newsitem.title: FRANCE: French voters' choice looks clear, but is it?.
newsitem.headline: French voters' choice looks clear, but is it?.

text.p: France's centre-right government and left-wing opposition have set out a sharp choice for voters on the key issues of economic policy and the role of the state, but neither side's position may be quite as clear as it seems.
Their platforms for the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election do not bear too much resemblance to their record in government.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe offered a vision of tax cutting, continuing privatisation, reducing the role of the state and sticking strictly to the rules for a single European currency in his keynote speech on Tuesday.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin stressed the need for a strong state, pledged to create 700,000 jobs -- half of them in the public sector -- ruled out further privatisation and rejected extra austerity to qualify for European monetary union because of France's record unemployment.

He has also called for a national conference on wages, jobs and reducing of working hours, advocating a gradual shift to a 35-hour work week without loss of pay. The centre-right has ruled out any across-the-board cut in the work week.
But political analysts say both leaders have staked out opening positions designed to unite their own camp, and both are likely to edge towards the centre ground in the weeks ahead.
Juppe has set a moderately conservative economic agenda and been careful to rule out the more radical Thatcherite deregulation which the left charges the coalition is planning.
He stressed his attachment to France's generous welfare state and to its public services.

Juppe's government has raised the tax burden to a record level over the last two years, blaming the need to "pay off Socialist debts", and added to the jungle of employment subsidies which he now pledges to simplify.

Commentator Laurent Mauduit wrote in the newspaper Le Monde that Juppe appeared to be renewing the double-talk of President Jacques Chirac's 1995 presidential campaign, which featured promises to cut taxes, create jobs and raise wages.
"With the opening of a new election campaign, is this method of equivocation back again?" he asked.

Although Jospin has sounded more sceptical on the terms for European economic and monetary union (EMU), partly to conciliate the Communist party with whom he is negotiating an electoral pact, he has stressed he supports the euro.

It was a Socialist president, Francois Mitterrand, who negotiated the Maastricht treaty setting the criteria for a single currency, and many of Juppe's Gaullist supporters voted against it in a 1992 referendum.

The Socialists have has set four conditions for EMU -- creating a "European government" as a counterweight to an independent central bank; ensuring that Mediterranean states, especially Italy and Spain, join from the start; agreeing on an EU pact for solidarity and growth; and ensuring the euro is not overvalued against the dollar.
Those may look like an attempt to rewrite the treaty, but EU diplomats say they probably should not be taken too literally.
If the Left won, Jospin would share power with Chirac. In previous bouts of left-right "cohabitation", the president has been dominant in setting European policy, they noted.
Nevertheless, the French Socialists have staked out an economic policy well to the left of their comrades in Britain, Germany, Italy or Spain.
